title: Letter by letter
hook: spelling a name, you go letter by letter; do each duty in order (Meditations 6.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rusticus, and the emperor who invited correction. Your line was show me. Did you change a mind, your own? Day five hundred eighty.

You're on the phone with customer service, spelling your last name. The agent gets it wrong. You spell it again, slowly. Wrong again, a different letter this time. Now there's a little heat in your voice, and the letters start coming out louder, as if volume could fix it. Marcus Aurelius uses this very moment, spelling a name aloud, as a picture for how to get through a whole day's work.

First, the scene. In Meditations six, twenty-six, Marcus says: suppose someone asks you how to write the name Antoninus. That was the name of his adoptive father. Do you shout each letter at him? And if he gets angry, do you get angry back? No. You just go on, calmly, counting off the letters one at a time. Second, the lesson. So it is in life, he says. Every duty is made up of certain parts, like a name is made of letters. Notice them. Do them in order. Third, the part about anger. Marcus adds that you should keep going without being disturbed, and without showing anger toward people who are angry with you. That's the phone call. The other person's frustration doesn't change the next letter. You still say N, then T, then O. Getting louder just adds another angry person to the line. Fourth, why it works. A whole duty can feel huge and blurry. A tax return. A hard conversation. A move. Broken into letters, each piece is small enough to say clearly. And there's an odd calm in it. When you're on the letter T, you don't have to be on the letter S. You just have to say T well. Marcus isn't describing a productivity trick. He's describing a temper. The person who goes letter by letter is less likely to lose their head, because they always know exactly what comes next.
screen: `HOW DO YOU SPELL ANTONINUS?` · `EVERY DUTY HAS ITS LETTERS.` · `DON'T SHOUT BACK.` · `ONE LETTER IS SMALL ENOUGH.` · then, large: `LETTER BY LETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Pick one task waiting for you today that feels too big or tangled. Now break it into letters. What's the very first piece? The second? The third? Name three, slowly, in your mind. Don't do them yet. Just see them in order, like letters in a name. Then come back to the breath, one at a time, in and out, letter by letter. The bell holds the time.
Antoninus, the name Marcus imagined spelling calmly, letter by letter, even if the person asking grew impatient. Today's word.
Your line: one letter at a time. Today, take that tangled task and finish just the first letter, then the next, all the way through. Day five hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 580 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEEN THE PRESENT, SEEN ALL.`

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use 'letter by letter' for large or stressful work: breaking a duty into its parts and doing each in order, without matching the impatience of people around them.

fork.setup: someone asks you to spell a name, gets it wrong, and snaps at you. what does Marcus say you do?
options: calmly go on, one letter at a time.
fork.reveal: Meditations 6.26: you don't shout or get angry; you count off each letter, and so you should do every duty.

original.note: Greek: letters of the alphabet, the parts a written name is made of.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient productivity tip.
what it means: breaking a duty into its letters keeps your temper as well as your focus.
what a scholar hears: Antoninus was also the name of the adoptive father Marcus calls a model elsewhere in the Meditations (1.16, 6.30), so the example comes from his own household.

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): cut 'everyone has been there', the adoption date (138) and the claim that Marcus bore the name, and the 'grammar' etymology. The identification of Antoninus in 6.26 with Antoninus Pius is historical, not stated in 6.26; Keeper to confirm it may stand.

Meditations 6.26 paraphrased: asked how to write the name Antoninus, would you shout each letter, and get angry if he's angry? You count off each letter; so every duty is made of parts; go on without being disturbed or angry at the angry. Confirm.
Marcus was adopted by Antoninus Pius in AD 138 and took the name Antoninus; confirm date and naming.
